core: Working definition of social stratification: a society's categorization of its people into rankings based on wealth, income, education, family background, and power; layers represent the uneven distribution of resources
Three named systems of stratification, one factual line each: slavery, caste, class
Closed vs open systems of stratification (fixed position vs mobility)
Davis-Moore functionalist thesis vs Marx's conflict view of stratification, one line each
Social mobility: movement between layers, with the honest note that mobility varies and is not as common or easy as many think
Intersectionality: layers overlap (term attributed to Kimberlé Crenshaw)
Honest framing: stratification is the skeleton of inequality
supporting: Socioeconomic status (SES) as an individual's place within stratification
The geological strata metaphor behind the term stratification
Upward/downward, intergenerational/intragenerational, and structural mobility distinctions
Tumin's (1953) criticism of the Davis-Moore thesis as evidence the theory is contested

claims.claim: Social stratification refers to a society's categorization of its people into rankings based on factors like wealth, income, education, family background, and power; a society's layers, made of people, represent the uneven distribution of society's resources.

Sociologists distinguish closed systems of stratification, which accommodate little change in social position and do not permit social relationships between levels (estate, slavery, and caste systems), from open systems, which are based on achievement and allow movement and interaction between layers and classes.

Historically, slavery is a condition in which one human being was owned by another; a slave was considered by law as property, or chattel, and was deprived of most of the rights ordinarily held by free persons.

Caste systems are closed stratification systems in which people can do little or nothing to change the social standing of their birth; the caste system determines all aspects of an individual's life, including occupations, marriage partners, and housing.

A class system is based on both social factors and individual achievement; a class consists of a set of people who share similar status based on factors like wealth, income, education, family background, and occupation, and unlike caste systems, class systems are open.

The Davis-Moore thesis (1945) argued that the greater the functional importance of a social role, the greater must be the reward, so that stratification represents the inherently unequal value of different work; Melvin Tumin (1953) criticized it, arguing stratification prevented qualified people from attempting to fill roles.

Conflict theorists are deeply critical of social stratification, asserting that it benefits only some people, not all of society; drawing on Karl Marx, they see stratification as resulting from people's relationship to production — owners (the bourgeoisie) versus workers (the proletariat) — with the resulting inequality creating class conflict.

Social mobility refers to the ability of individuals to change positions within a social stratification system; people can move upward or downward, across generations (intergenerational mobility) or within a lifetime (intragenerational mobility), and whole groups can move together through structural mobility.
Scholars recognize that social mobility is not as common or easy to achieve as many people think.

The term intersectionality was coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in her 1989 article 'Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex'; intersectionality emphasizes that different dimensions of identity are not isolated from one another but intertwine and overlap, resulting in distinct advantages or disadvantages.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Why do the layers of stratification exist: functional necessity or domination?
positions: Davis and Moore (1945): the greater the functional importance of a social role, the greater must be the reward; stratification represents the inherently unequal value of different work.
Melvin Tumin (1953): stratification actually prevented qualified people from attempting to fill roles.
Conflict theorists drawing on Marx: stratification benefits only some people, not all of society; it grows out of the relationship to production and creates class conflict.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both attributed positions plus the criticism without endorsing any of them; each is stated at one-line depth per the topic's scope.
